heroStories.title: The Women Behind Some of MENA’s Biggest Companies
heroStories.excerpt: Trendyol is one of Turkey’s biggest technology companies. Insider sells its software to more than 1,500 brands across 28 countries. Huda Beauty became a global cosmetics business, while Hepsiburada became the first Turkish company to list on Nasdaq. Across MENA, women have helped build some of the region’s largest companies in e-commerce, enterprise software, beauty, logistics, fintech and investing.

heroStories.title: How Peak Games Became a Starting Point for Turkey’s Next Gaming Companies
heroStories.excerpt: In 2019, five employees left Peak Games to build another mobile gaming company in Istanbul. Today, Peak Games alumni have built some of the highest grossing casual puzzle games in mobile history, establishing Istanbul as a global gaming superpower.

heroStories.title: What It Takes to Take a Gulf Restaurant Brand Abroad
heroStories.excerpt: At Harrods in London, Somewhere serves guacamole hummus, kunafa-wrapped shrimp and beef shawarma with beetroot rice. Homegrown Gulf concepts are now exporting regional flavors and hospitality tech across European and Asian capitals.

heroStories.title: Tabby vs Tamara: The Competition Is Moving Beyond Buy Now, Pay Later
heroStories.excerpt: Tabby and Tamara became familiar to Gulf shoppers through a simple offer: buy something now and spread the payment across instalments. But with combined billions in valuation, the battle is shifting to everyday consumer banking and debit cards.

heroStories.title: Why Gulf Startups Are Building Around the Corner Shop
heroStories.excerpt: A neighbourhood shop can look like a small customer for a technology company. Across the Gulf, local baqalas process tens of billions in cash, making them the primary battleground for B2B tech and credit infrastructure.

founders.bio: Former Accenture consultant whose Nabta Health blends digital tools with conventional care for women

body.text: We adapted. We survived.

Sophie Smith read history at the University of Cambridge and holds an MBA from the Quantic School of Business and Technology. She spent four years as a technology consultant at Accenture and founded several ventures, among them myZindagi, a platform for finding doctors in Pakistan, as well as Synnapps and SNS Consulting. She also co-founded 22Four. In March 2017 she founded Nabta Health, which is headquartered in Sharjah. Nabta describes its model as hybrid, combining fertility tracking, at-home testing, virtual consultations and a machine-learning personal assistant to help women identify, manage and prevent non-communicable diseases. Its first care pathway focused on PCOS, with the stated aim of making a diagnosis possible in under 90 days. In June 2020 the company reported that it served 250,000 women a month and had reached 18 million women through health-awareness campaigns since January 2018.

Today Trase serves 25 enterprise clients on 113 live projects across Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Egypt and Morocco. Rowan is an IVLP alumna, a leading woman in tech, ConTech Leader of the Year 2026, TiE Women MENA 2026 winner and a CICA ConTech Laureate.

founders.name: Lauren Hamilton
founders.hook: Started Ride Skipper, a UAE chauffeur service using customers' own cars, after a C-section
founders.bio: Started Ride Skipper, a UAE chauffeur service using customers' own cars, after a C-section

body.text: I've spent two years proving the thesis that when drivers have job security and financial stability, versus the traditional gig economy model, they show up naturally calmer and safer behind the wheel. I'm excited for the next phase of growth we're entering, scaling the business to meet overwhelming demand.

Lauren Hamilton spent ten years in sales and partnerships roles in the hotel industry before she ran into a problem first-hand that she couldn't stop thinking about. After a C-section left her unable to drive, she could not find a service in Dubai she trusted to carry her son safely, and the more she learned about the existing landscape, the more sure she was that it could be done differently, and better. She launched Ride Skipper in 2024, providing vetted professional drivers who drive customers in their own cars, and is its founder and general manager. Her thesis is that drivers with job security and financial stability, rather than the traditional gig-economy model, are calmer and safer behind the wheel. According to a 2026 speaker profile, in 18 months the business grew from six drivers taking bookings over WhatsApp to more than 30 drivers and a mobile app, and it is now scaling to meet demand.

career: Founder and General Manager, Ride Skipper

founders.name: Caroline Hazlehurst
founders.hook: Scaling executive; former Moove President and Calo COO, now Co-Founder and CEO of Base, AI infrastructure for business operations.
founders.bio: Scaling executive; former Moove President and Calo COO, now Co-Founder and CEO of Base, AI infrastructure for business operations.

body.text: I've spent my career scaling PE and venture-backed technology companies as President, COO and regional VP, and I've seen how much work sits between building a product and running a business. Founders need context across customers, contracts, finance and people, but it's scattered across separate tools. With Base, we're building AI infrastructure for running your business; applied AI tools that sit on top of a system of intelligence that brings context and persistent memory together. We want to do for running a business what vibe coding did for building a product: close the gap between having an idea and making it happen, so founders can spend less time managing complexity and more time building their vision.

Caroline Hazlehurst is a growth and operating executive with 12 years scaling venture-backed technology companies as President, COO and regional VP, three of which reached unicorn valuations. She scaled Moove globally, took Bird EMEA from 0 to 90+ cities in 18 months, prepared Calo for IPO, and ran more than half of Deliveroo's global business. She has built and led organisations of 1,500+ people. Now Co-Founder and CEO of Base, Caroline is building AI infrastructure for business operations that connects a company's tool stack and resolves it into one queryable company brain, built on a knowledge graph. Her earlier career was in private equity at Bridgepoint and M&A at Rothschild.

Hatem Kameli studied computer science at King AbdulAziz University, graduating in 2007. In November 2013 he founded iCLICK, a digital marketing consultancy, and ran it as CEO until December 2017. Saad Ahmed has spent his career on one problem: how money moves between businesses and the people they serve. Raised in Bahrain, he studied business, management and marketing at the New York Institute of Technology, then worked at Red Bull and FP7 McCann before leading projects across MENA at PwC. He left to found Retroban Middle East, growing it from 10 people to more than 40, and then RBW Fintech Services, where he built BWallet, Bahrain's first peer-to-peer digital wallet, working with regulators, banks, telecom operators and merchants. BWallet became the largest P2P digital wallet in Bahrain and Oman, signing more than 6,000 merchants and serving 100,000 customers in four years before he exited. Along the way he founded LocalBH Media Group (LocalBH, LocalRYDH, LocalDubai and more), a digital media network now reaching tens of millions of people a month across eight cities in Bahrain, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

Local brings it all together. In restaurants, hotels and hospitals, paying is never a single moment. It is a chain of checkpoints: waiting for the bill, waiting for a card machine, queueing at a cashier, splitting, tipping, reconciling. Each one costs the customer time and the business revenue. Local collapses that chain into one flow on the customer's own phone: scan, see what you owe, pay in seconds, with no app, no terminal and no queue. Because it plugs straight into the systems merchants already run, Local sits at the centre of the business rather than at its edge, opening the door to lending, loyalty and customer data that a card machine never could.

Launched in June 2025, Local signed more than 250 merchants in its first year and operates across the UAE and Bahrain, with Saudi Arabia launching next. Merchants see higher order values, and staff take home more in tips because Local charges no fees on them. It started in restaurants, where the pain is most visible, and has already built a working prototype for hospital queues, billing and patient flow. Local has raised close to USD 3M at seed from 500 Global Sanabil, 21VC and VentureSouq.

body.text: Alexander Pinheiro Liakos is co-founder and CEO of Mifta, an AI-powered rental brokerage in Dubai, and was named one of MENA's Founding 30 for 2026. He began his career as one of the first hires at ThreeWire, a clinical-trial recruitment company later acquired by WIRB-Copernicus Group, then moved into venture capital, investing in early-stage US-based technology companies. He later founded a hospitality real estate venture in Mykonos, Greece, before joining Antler's founder program in Dubai, where Mifta was born. Today he is rebuilding how people rent homes, bringing search, viewings, negotiation, paperwork and payment into one seamless digital journey.

founders.hook: Built a grocery delivery startup acquired by X5, now turning shelf photos into retail decisions
founders.bio: Built a grocery delivery startup acquired by X5, now turning shelf photos into retail decisions

body.text: We've built a grocery delivery service from scratch in Russia. For 2 years (starting 2017), we were scaling it ourselves

Daniel Alimov is the co-founder and CEO of Retailhub, the Dubai-based company bringing AI to grocery retail. Retailhub helps retailers, FMCG brands and aggregators fix product availability and out-of-stock problems, a $1 trillion-a-year drain on the industry. It works in partnership with Talabat, the region's largest delivery platform and part of the Delivery Hero group, and is scaling fast across the GCC.

Already operating in five markets, the platform processes hundreds of thousands of shelf images a day. In live stores the impact shows within months: orders with out-of-stock items drop two to three times while active online assortment grows. Retailhub is backed by Oraseya Capital, 21 Ventures, the former CEOs of Talabat and Majid Al Futtaim Carrefour, Hub71, Google AI and others.

Daniel is a serial founder with an exit behind him. In Kazan he built Dostavushka, a grocery delivery service, into the city's number-one e-grocery player within five months, then sold it to X5 Group, the retailer behind Pyaterochka and Perekrestok. He joined X5 as head of new business development to roll grocery delivery out nationally, a business that now processes around $1.5 billion in annual GMV. He moved to the UAE in 2021 and built Retailhub to solve the problems he faced daily at Dostavushka and X5.
He trained in law, with a bachelor's degree from the University of London and a master's in international law, and was head of legal at a major infrastructure engineering firm by 22.

body.text: India is one of the fastest-growing e-commerce markets in the world, and its logistics sector is going through a major shift - service providers are getting more sophisticated, building their own end-to-end networks, and going after the global market.

Denis Konoplev studied international business at Grenoble Ecole de Management and took an MSc in management of information systems and digital innovation at the London School of Economics. He co-founded Disperse, an AI startup for construction built on computer vision. He was later co-founder, COO and head of product at Seafood Souq, and head of product at Further Ventures. At RSA Global he worked as director of product and as digital transformation manager before moving to RSA Cross Border, which he co-founded and has led as CEO since December 2025, according to his profile. RSA XB is a spin-out building software-first logistics for cross-border e-commerce, starting with routes from India to the UK, Europe and the GCC. In 2026 it announced a $1.5 million seed round, to be deployed over 18 months, and reported 10% week-over-week growth in the 12 months before the May 2026 announcement.

body.text: Push really doesn’t work at all. Pull does.

Khalifa Manaa describes himself as from Finland and based in Dubai. He has been described as a product specialist, startup mentor, venture builder and occasional angel investor. He founded Shapr, where he was CEO, and before that co-founded RideHoop. He has mentored founders at Next Level and on in5 Dubai's Build your Startup with AI programme. In July 2024 he co-founded Sampo AI with Saif Al-Essai. Now trading as Sampo Pricing, the company offers competitor price monitoring, pricing recommendations and automated repricing for e-commerce retailers, with integrations including Shopify, WooCommerce, Salla and Zid. In January 2025 Sampo announced a $750,000 pre-seed round co-led by Omantel Innovation Labs and Waad VC, with Hexnture and Saudi angel investors taking part; the company called it the largest pre-seed investment in Oman. At the time it reported a database of more than 10 million regional products, and its website cites an average 22% rise in customer margins.

articles.title: The Women Behind Some of MENA’s Biggest Companies
articles.description: Trendyol is one of Turkey’s biggest technology companies. Insider sells its software to more than 1,500 brands across 28 countries. Huda Beauty became a global cosmetics business, while Hepsiburada became the first Turkish company to list on Nasdaq.
articles.lead: Trendyol is one of Turkey’s biggest technology companies. Insider sells its software to more than 1,500 brands across 28 countries. Huda Beauty became a global cosmetics business, while Hepsiburada became the first Turkish company to list on Nasdaq. They were built in different cities, across different industries, and at very different moments in the region’s startup history. But each had a woman on the founding team.

sections.heading: The first generation built category-defining companies
paragraphs: Some of the region’s earliest venture-backed giants were built by women, starting in e-commerce and consumer platforms.

Demet Mutlu co-founded Trendyol in 2010. The company became an online powerhouse, eventually backed by Alibaba, that reached a $16.5 billion valuation in 2021 and created thousands of jobs across Turkey.
Hanzade Dogan founded Hepsiburada around 2000, steering the company into a dominant marketplace that listed on Nasdaq in 2021 — the first Turkish business to achieve that milestone.

Mona Ataya and Leena Khalil co-founded Mumzworld in 2011 to solve a regional parenting gap. It grew into one of the Middle East’s leading mother-and-baby retail networks before its acquisition by Tamer Group in 2021.

sections.heading: The next wave moved into software and infrastructure
paragraphs: The newer generation looks very different, tackling enterprise software, logistics and core fintech infrastructure.

Hande Cilingir co-founded Insider in Istanbul to help brands predict customer behaviour and personalise marketing. The company has since grown into a major enterprise software business serving more than 1,500 brands across 28 countries, including Nike, L’Oréal, Toyota and Disney.

In Dubai, Rita Huang and Nancy Chen co-founded iMile around another problem created by the region’s digital economy: last-mile delivery. The company has since expanded across 30 countries and raised more than $100 million.

Qlub took on a different piece of infrastructure. Co-founded by Gizem Bodur as part of a larger founding team, the Dubai-based company built ultra-fast in-restaurant payment systems and quickly scaled across multiple continents.

sections.heading: Fintech has become one of the strongest clusters
paragraphs: Several of the companies on the list sit in financial services, transforming everyday consumer and corporate finance.

Khazna was co-founded by Fatma Shafiq to build financial products for Egyptians underserved by traditional banks. Ziina, co-founded by Sara Toukan, built around mobile payments, making it easier for users to send and receive money across the UAE.
Sarwa, co-founded by Nadine Mezher, made investing more accessible by giving ordinary users access to automated wealth management.

sections.heading: Most of these companies were built by teams
paragraphs: It is also important to be precise about what “founded by women” means. Many of these businesses were not built by solo female founders, but by teams with complementary skills.

Several women here were one member of a larger founding team, often alongside men. That does not weaken the significance of their role — it reflects how large companies are usually built: by teams with different responsibilities and expertise.

sections.heading: The scene is becoming harder to overlook
paragraphs: The numbers attached to these companies are significant: Trendyol reached $16.5 billion in its 2021 round, while Insider was valued at $2.5 billion in 2024.

What connects them is that the companies themselves have become difficult to ignore, making the story less about “women-founded startups” as a separate category, and more about who is building the region’s most enduring institutions.

articles.title: How Peak Games Became a Starting Point for Turkey’s Next Gaming Companies
articles.description: In 2019, five employees left Peak Games to build another mobile gaming company in Istanbul. Today, Peak Games alumni have founded dozens of mobile studios across Istanbul, turning the city into a global gaming hub.
articles.lead: In 2019, five employees left Peak Games to build another mobile gaming company in Istanbul. When Zynga acquired Peak Games for $1.8 billion in 2020, it confirmed Turkey’s gaming potential. But the bigger story was what Peak’s early team did next.

sections.heading: The mafia effect in Istanbul gaming
paragraphs: Like PayPal in Silicon Valley or Careem in Dubai, Peak Games produced an extraordinary founder ecosystem.

Former Peak executives and developers went on to launch Dream Games, Spyke Games, Bigger Games and Loop Games. Together, these studios have raised hundreds of millions of dollars and produced hit titles played by tens of millions worldwide.

sections.heading: Dream Games and the Royal Match phenomenon
paragraphs: Founded by former Peak product director Soner Aydemir and four colleagues, Dream Games created Royal Match, which became one of the highest-grossing mobile puzzle games globally, catapulting Dream Games to a $2.75 billion valuation in record time.
The studio proved that Istanbul was not a one-hit wonder, but a repeatable hub for casual mobile puzzle excellence.

articles.lead: At Harrods in London, Somewhere serves guacamole hummus, kunafa-wrapped shrimp and beef shawarma with beetroot rice. For decades, the Gulf was purely an importer of international dining concepts. Now, a wave of homegrown culinary brands is reversing the flow.

sections.heading: From Dubai to Knightsbridge
paragraphs: Concepts born in Dubai, Riyadh and Kuwait City are finding enthusiastic audiences in European capitals.
Operating abroad requires mastering complex European supply chains, international staffing and strict regulatory environments while maintaining the generous, luxury service ethos of Gulf hospitality.

sections.heading: The rise of regional food tech and cloud kitchens
paragraphs: Backing this international push is a sophisticated regional ecosystem of food tech, ghost kitchen operations like Kitopi, and advanced procurement technology that makes cross-border scaling viable.

articles.title: Tabby vs Tamara: The Competition Is Moving Beyond Buy Now, Pay Later
articles.description: Tabby and Tamara became familiar to Gulf shoppers through a simple offer: buy something now and spread the payment across instalments. Now they are locked in a fight for everyday banking, digital wallets and merchant software.
articles.lead: Tabby and Tamara became household names across Saudi Arabia and the UAE by offering a straightforward promise: interest-free instalment shopping. But buy now, pay later was only the entry ticket.

sections.heading: From checkout buttons to full financial ecosystems
paragraphs: Both unicorns have recently expanded into debit cards, digital accounts, cash-back reward programs, and merchant lending solutions.
Tabby’s $6.5 billion valuation and Tamara’s Saudi market leadership set the stage for one of the fiercest fintech duels in emerging markets.

sections.heading: Profitability and credit performance
paragraphs: Unlike many Western BNPL players that struggled with loss rates, both Gulf platforms have demonstrated profitability through tight risk algorithms and strong merchant relationships.
